On November fifth, California's governor announced he would commute all 548 death sentences in his state.

America has emptied its death rows before.

June twenty-ninth, 1972. In Furman versus Georgia, the Supreme Court voted five to four. Forty state death penalty laws were voided. 629 people had their death sentences commuted.

Justice Potter Stewart said those sentences were cruel and unusual "in the same way that being struck by lightning is cruel and unusual."

It didn't last. Thirty-five states wrote new laws. In 1976, the Court approved them, seven to two.

And in California, most of the new commutations need the state Supreme Court's approval.

The full file is on the channel. The American File.
